### 1.9 Test-Time Scaling &amp; Inference Algorithms

#### [Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33896>)

Floodgates trains low-rank adapters on one shared loop to draft several future tokens from deep prefix states, then verifies the block with the full model. It reports 3.0–8.2× greedy speedups over plain decoding in its single-A100 tests, offering a practical acceleration path for looped models while requiring trained adapters and careful numerical verification.

#### [FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34492>)

FlyingStart fits a linear map from the previous token’s exit state and the current input to initialize a frozen recurrent-depth model, leaving its iteration and stopping rule unchanged. On Huginn-0125 it reports 14–19% fewer decoding layers at matched math accuracy and 16–18% higher batched throughput, suggesting a cheap calibration route whose benefit narrows on faster-converging models and other task formats.

## AI Training &amp; Inference Infra

### 3.3 Inference Engines &amp; Serving

#### [RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33542>)

RankCast balances expert-parallel MoE serving against different bottlenecks: peak token load during prefill and peak active-expert count during decode. It overlaps next-layer routing prediction and compact load metadata with existing DeepEP communication, then adjusts rank prices or closes selected experts to reduce stragglers. On two Qwen deployments using H800 GPUs, prefill input throughput improves by up to 19.4% and median decode time per output token falls, with measured quality changes below one percentage point rather than lossless routing.

#### [PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34615>)

PipeAxes uses wide prefill batches but yields between layer slices, allowing decode requests to run without repeatedly loading every layer’s weights for small token chunks. It separately sizes compressed activation row groups and prioritizes short transfers, giving the scheduler independent control over GPU occupancy and network blocking. Physical-GPU replays with shaped Ethernet links show 1.17–2.16× the goodput of a calibrated Revisit-PP port in the tested two-stage WAN sweep; the gains depend on workload, latency targets and lossy INT4 transport.

[Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/new?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>) · [Timing source](<https://blog.arxiv.org/2026/11/25/holiday-announcement-schedule/>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34615v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Read all scientific text on pages 1–10 through Availability in the 13-page manuscript; the remaining text is references, with no scientific appendix. Source pages 7 and 9 were directly viewed. LayerSpool retains batch/KV metadata and intermediate tensors, resumes prefill at layer boundaries, isolates decode CUDA graphs and gates decode on consumed-row watermarks. A Hadamard-INT4 codec merges hidden and residual tensors; independently sized activation row groups travel on striped TCP with express-frame priority. Affine startup calibration and online recursive least squares guide batch width, slice depth and transport groups. Experiments use BF16 Qwen3-8B, 30B-A3B and 32B, two 80 GB PCIe A800s without NVLink/P2P, and two 24 GB RTX 4090s plus two 24 GB RTX 3090s over 1 GbE. Linux netem shapes 100–1,000 Mbps and 30 ms RTT, with optional jitter/loss. Baselines share vLLM 0.23.0 V2 and kernels; Revisit-PP is the authors’ calibrated port and uses the same compressed priority transport on WAN. Across 97 paired replays and 5,016 requests, goodput requires all TTFT, TPOT and per-request p95 inter-token targets; target values and coding-agent multipliers depend on workload. The two-stage 8B/250 Mbps sweep reports 1.17–2.16× Revisit-PP goodput and 1.30–2.33× the best static grid. One bandwidth-swing run meets 74/74 targets versus 46/74; a separate four-stage MoE stress replay meets 16/21 versus 1/21, yielding 23.3× goodput from unrounded rates. The mixed 64K 32B case meets all fifteen short-request targets, but eight long requests miss the 12-second TTFT objective because computation alone exceeds fourteen seconds. INT4 quality is tested on Qwen3-8B: MMLU 75.02→75.08%, GSM8K 90.30→89.84%, and a 24-prompt SCBench subset 15→16 correct. The original November 26 DC batch and official schedule infer announcement on November 26 at 01:00 UTC. The paper promises future code and replay logs; no author release was verified.

**Limitations:** These are shaped-link experiments on physical GPUs, not measurements of a geographically deployed WAN. Large goodput ratios can have only 9, 21 or 23 requests and very small baseline denominators. Individual tail latencies still miss targets under overload; the 74-request success does not establish a universal SLO guarantee. Prefix caching is disabled and only selected Qwen models/topologies are implemented. INT4 transport is lossy; quality evaluation covers one 8B model with limited uncertainty reporting and only 24 long-context retrieval prompts. Fixed-512 can complete coding sessions faster while violating token-latency objectives. Agent replays use extracted lengths/timing and prescribed turn spacing, rather than closed-loop coding success. Code and raw logs are promised rather than verified; no independent experiments were run.

### 3.5 Kernels, Compilers &amp; Runtimes

#### [NVFP4 Attention: New Matched Kernel and World-Model Measurements of Existing Register Recycling](<https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/how-to-optimize-nvfp4-attention-on-nvidia-rtx-blackwell-through-register-recycling/>)

This new evaluation separates an existing NVFP4 attention kernel’s register-recycling gains from the overhead and benefits of integrating low-precision attention into complete world models. Matched-input tests on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell report 1.17–1.64× core-kernel speedups, while separately measured BF16-to-NVFP4 model paths reduce generation or action latency by 1.11–15.34%. The practical lesson is to reuse retired score storage and select compatible attention calls carefully; these measurements do not establish a new kernel release, universal quality preservation or serving-wide speedup.

**Published:** 2026-11-25 · **First seen:** 2026-11-27T11:03:46.387+00:00 · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Attention Kernels, Register Reuse, NVFP4

[Blog](<https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/how-to-optimize-nvfp4-attention-on-nvidia-rtx-blackwell-through-register-recycling/>) · [Code](<https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4502>) · [Project](<https://www.reactor.inc/blog/nvfp4-attention-world-models>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Read both complete November 25 NVIDIA and Reactor articles, all pseudocode, Tables 1–2, benchmark conditions, integration rules and qualitative quality caveats. The proposed contribution is the newly disclosed evaluation, not the optimization’s invention or release. Linked FlashInfer PR 4502 was created August 13 and merged August 25; it already describes symmetric N64/N64 score-slot reuse and four H8 timing rows that compare against previously reported baselines rather than a matched run. The immutable merged mainloop and benchmark were retrieved. Critical mainloop lines 648–918 show retired score-slot refill, full-N128 online-softmax preparation and separate drain; benchmark defaults and configuration/timing sections establish the older H8 protocol. No code was executed. The November article instead tests batch 1, 24 heads, dimension 128 and equal Q/K lengths of 4,096, 7,040, 8,192 and 16,384 tokens on one 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120). Original and optimized NVFP4 kernels receive identical inputs, packed tensors and LSE settings, measured with three fresh processes per implementation, alternating order, prewarming and repeated CUDA-event blocks. Core latency excludes input quantization and output-stride restoration. The eight cells yield 1.17–1.64×; captured LongLive noncausal latency is 0.75052→0.63548 ms. Separate full model paths compare BF16 cuDNN attention with selected NVFP4 calls while model weights remain BF16, including quantization, conversion and decoded CPU frames/action output, but excluding load, warmup, network, queueing and client pacing. Long-run LongLive and Helios use three independent processes per arm; OmniDreams uses one process per arm/scenario. The largest 15.34% reduction is a 2,045-frame/256-chunk moving-camera OmniDreams case, 155.92→132.00 seconds; Helios changes are only 1.11–1.78%. Reactor documents per-model shape/mask/padding/GQA checks, selected-call coverage and manual visual/simulation quality observations. The August PR contains neither these H24 matched measurements nor the four-model integration study. November 25 article publication metadata and dated companion are retained; no exact global first-visibility instant is inferred. No matching source is covered in the complete registry and the exact article slug is absent from prior November 24/25 native indexes.

**Limitations:** The kernel method and software predate the window. Novelty is the new controlled measurement and integration study; an August merge alone is not proof of the exact earlier public-visibility instant. Kernel-only matched comparisons and end-to-end BF16-to-NVFP4 comparisons answer different questions: the latter combine quantization, backend, call-selection and integration effects and do not isolate register recycling. End-to-end timing excludes networking/queueing and is not a production serving latency or cost guarantee. Most shapes are synthetic, with one captured LongLive shape, and only one RTX Blackwell model is tested. OmniDreams long-run results have one process per arm. Quality assessment is manual visual review and manual RoboLab simulation, with no specified sample count, blinded metric or statistical guarantee. Coverage percentages count attention matrix-multiplication FLOPs, not total model work or GPU time. Unsupported calls remain BF16. No independent reproduction or execution was performed.
